doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Coltrane's lesson about respecting musicians
summary: Ali tells how he put down a musician to Coltrane and learned to always listen for something good.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Was there other things besides just the music that you gained from him also?

Yeah, I gained how to be a better person. I know I gained — because I had a pretty — I had an ego. I was completely egotistical when I was coming up. I felt like, you know, I was playing with Coltrane, I was the best that ever lived, you know, I was the only thing that ever happened on this earth you know, because I was working with the greatest saxophonist in the world. And I felt like I was all that. And there’s a story I used to tell, I told Coltrane once, he asked me about this musician. You know, he said, “Rashied there’s a musician out there asking me to sit in,” you know, and he said, “and he also said that he had played with you before.” And he said, “What do you think, what do you think?” you know. He always used to come at me with stuff like that. “What do you think, should I let him play” or something. And I said, “Oh man, that cat can’t play shit,” you know. And he said, “Oh really?” I said, “Man, he ain’t playing shit man.” You know what he did when he went out on the bandstand, the first thing he did was say, “Hey man, come on up and play.” And I felt like I wanted to disappear behind the drumset. I felt too bad because I put the cat down without even thinking about anything. And I was very quiet for the rest of the night, I wasn’t saying anything to nobody. And he said, “You know” (I’m not going to mention his name, he’s not here anymore anyways) he said, “you know,” he © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

said, “what do you think about this guy” who was playing. Of course I wasn’t going to say anything else bad about him. I said, “Well you know.” He said, “Well you know, Rashied,” he said “I’m going to tell you man,” he said, “I don’t care how bad or how good you think a person is playing music. I say if he’s playing music” he said “there’s always something you can get out of it if you listen. It might not be something you can use, but it might be something you can use, I mean I don’t care how bad you think he plays or whatever, but there could be something there that you can get from it if you listen.” And I never went at a person like that again. You know I never talked bad about a person since then. Because, so I mean I learned a lot of stuff from John, as to how to be as a person. And you know, give people a break. Don’t talk down on musicians, especially if it’s about music. So I learned quite a bit from him as a youngster coming up. And it works for me too, because I have a lot of respect for everybody and you learn a lot when you respect people. Because you’re not closed minded. You don’t think like you know, because I feel like when you’re closed minded and think you’re all that, that’s when I think you stop learning. You can’t learn anything no more because you think you know everything. And then you start going that way instead of this way. As long as you keep your mind open, like John and Cecil Taylor and all those cats, they keep their mind open. They embrace what people are doing. They listen. And that’s how you become a great whatever-you-are trying to be behind just listening to people and being able to absorb stuff. And I learned that.
